text.p: President Suharto on Monday unveiled Indonesia's state budget for the coming fiscal year which aims to maintain the momentum of economic growth while curbing inflation and boosting exports.
For the first time in the country's history, the budget exceeded one hundred trillion rupiah ($42 billion).
The budget for fiscal 1997/98 from April 1 to March 31 continued with the tradition of allocating large amounts of money to improve the living conditions of the nation's 200 million people.
Suharto said 1996/97 economic growth was expected to be around the 8.2 percent figure of the previous year.
Industry and Trade Minister Tunky Ariwibowo has predicted growth of between 7.6 and 7.9 percent for the coming year.

Suharto, a retired army general who came to power in the mid-1960s and who has generally been credited with the country's impressive economic performance, also drew attention to the general elections scheduled for May.
"1997/98 is a political year. The mechanism of national leadership will reach its culmination in 1997/98. Normally as a festivity, the general election must bring happiness to all of us," he said.
"Therefore, we have to prevent the general election from becoming the contrary, namely creating anxiety and suffering for the people," he added.
The 1997/98 budget, which is required by law to be balanced, will expand by 11.6 percent over 1996/97 to 101.09 trillion rupiah.
In a budget briefing ahead of Suharto's speech, Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad said domestic revenues in 1997/98 were projected to rise by 12.6 percent to 88.06 trillion rupiah ($37 billion).

He said non-oil revenue was projected to increase by 14.2 percent while oil revenue was seen growing by 5.3 percent in 1997/98. Indonesia is Asia's sole member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
"This shows that our domestic revenue structure has become more healthy ... that our dependence on oil and gas has become less," he said.
Mar'ie said the government projected revenue from crude oil at 10.69 trillion rupiah ($4.5 billion) in 1997/98, up from 10.32 trillion rupiah ($4.3 billion) in 1996/97.
He said revenue from gas was expected to be 4.18 trillion rupiah ($1.8 billion) in 1997/98, up from 3.80 trillion rupiah ($1.6 billion).

Coordinating Minister for Economics and Finance Saleh Afiff told the briefing that the country's current account deficit was expected to be $9.798 billion in fiscal 1997/98, or some 4.0 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP).
He said the current account deficit was expected to be $8.823 billion in 1996/97, or 4.0 percent of GDP.
"This defict is quite big but it doesn't mean that it's not uncontrollable," Afiff added.
He said inflation was 6.47 percent in the 1996 calendar year, compared with 8.64 percent in 1995. Inflation was projected at six percent for 1997.
